title: Vishvamitra slips, and starts again
hookLine: a king sets out to become a great sage and loses his progress to desire, then to anger; Patanjali names the nine obstacles on that road
carry: nine obstacles, all part of the path
tomorrow: an arrow-maker doesn't look up. what is he teaching?
last: JAPA — SAY THE NAME, AND MEAN IT.

lines: A KING WANTS TO BE A SAGE.
TEN YEARS WITH MENAKA. A CURSE IN ANGER.
cards: Vishvamitra starts out as a king who wants a sage's wish-granting cow and can't take it by force. So he gives up his throne to become a sage himself. In the Ramayana's telling, it takes him ages.
Brahma names him a royal sage, and he's disappointed; he wanted more. He goes deeper, and the apsara Menaka arrives; ten years pass before he remembers what he came for.
He goes deeper still, loses his temper, curses the apsara Rambha, and his hard-won tapas drains away again.

teach.h: HE GOES BACK, AND BECOMES BRAHMARSHI.
teach.b: Each time, Valmiki says, he sees what happened, grieves it, and goes back to the forest.
At last he vows silence, holds back anger altogether, and after a long, fierce tapas Brahma names him a brahmarshi, the highest kind of seer, and his old rival Vasishtha greets him as one.
Hindus honor this same Vishvamitra as the seer of the Gayatri mantra, which many say every morning.
Patanjali, in sutra 1.30, names what comes in between: the antarayas, nine obstacles. Vyadhi, illness. Styana, dullness.
Alasya, laziness. Avirati, craving, the pull of the senses. Bhranti darshana, false seeing.
Alabdha bhumikatva, not reaching a stage. And anavasthitatva, reaching a stage and not holding it.
Vishvamitra's road reads like the last of these: stages reached, lost, and reached again. Sutra 1.31 adds signs in the body that come with them: pain, dejection, trembling, ragged breath.
And here is the teaching, plain and very Hindu: the obstacles are expected. The sutras don't treat slipping as proof you're unfit; they name it so you can recognize it and return.
The tradition made one of its greatest seers out of a man who slipped again and again. Today, that's a missed week of practice. Not, I'm bad at this.
That's illness, or that's number nine, and I'm back.

how: Yoga teachers often have students learn the nine antarayas by name, so that illness, doubt or a plateau can be recognized as a normal part of practice rather than a reason to quit.

o: an obstacle, what comes in between
a demon that blocks the path to God

p: reaching a stage and not holding it

s: Patanjali's obstacles are all moral failings
illness is the first one. the list is ordinary: body, mind and habit.
in the Ramayana, Vishvamitra loses his progress more than once before he becomes a brahmarshi
desire with Menaka, then anger at Rambha; each time he went back to his tapas.
sutra 1.31 lists signs in the body that come with the obstacles
pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, and ragged breathing.

games.q: you kept a practice for a month, then missed a week, and now it feels blown. by sutra 1.30 and Vishvamitra's story, what's true?
o: the slip proves you weren't meant for it.
slipping is one of the named obstacles: recognize it and return.
you have to start from zero with a harder practice.
games.why: anavasthitatva, not holding a stage you'd reached, is on Patanjali's list. Vishvamitra lost his progress more than once and became a brahmarshi.

practice: Rest on the breath, or on a name of God if you pray, and watch for the nine as they show up: dullness like a heavy fog, doubt asking what's the point, craving with a sudden thought of food or your phone.
Each time, name it kindly, there's doubt, and come back, the way Vishvamitra kept going back to the forest. If the breath turns ragged or restless, name that too, and return.

wordCard.voice: Antaraya, obstacle, literally what comes in between. Patanjali names nine, from illness and doubt to losing a stage you'd reached. Vishvamitra met them, and kept going.

orig.note: Sanskrit antarāya: obstacle, literally what comes in between. Patanjali names nine.

carryVoice: Your line: nine obstacles, all part of the path. Vishvamitra slipped, and started again. Day four hundred thirty-eight.
